newsitem.title: UK: Political risk lures the bravehearted to Russia.
newsitem.headline: Political risk lures the bravehearted to Russia.

text.p: Fund managers say they are receiving more requests for investment in Russia than ever before as clients speculate on its political future should Yeltsin's health deteriorate.

"We've been swamped with more calls than ever from clients wanting short-term investment," one global custody manager at a Luxembourg bank told Reuters, on the edge of an emerging markets conference in London.
Although experienced investors have been in Russia for some time already, it is the second wave that is coming in now, said Keith Swabe, Assistant Director for fixed income at West Merchant Bank.
Both debt and equity markets are looking more attractive than they have for some time.

The weekend announcement by a Kremlin doctor that President Boris Yeltsin may have had a third heart attack during the summer election campaign, and news his health was less sturdy than believed, have pushed valuations on Russian equities to outstandingly cheap levels, fund managers say.

On the debt side, one Russian bond trader said foreign investors played a big part in the auction earlier on Wednesday of six-month GKO Treasury bills, while Russian MinFin bonds are also seeing strong demand from abroad.
"Yields (on Russian debt) have already backed up to make investing there more attractive, but investors must be aware of the increased political risk," Swabe added.

Douglas Polunin, who manages nearly $80 million for the First Russian Frontiers Trust, said client demand had been increasing since the time of Russia's presidential elections, but added investors were interested more in the medium-term view.
"Since the elections there has been a general increase, yes," he told Reuters. "It's mostly medium-term, between three and five years."
The trust, listed on the London exchange, is currently seeking a second placing due to increased shareholder demand.
Another Russian fund manager agreed interest had shot up.

"Investor interest increased very sharply in the spring, especially before the elections," he said. "It is certainly more interesting when prices go down, and Russia's increasing openness to foreign investment is spurring people to look more seriously."
The question now is how to assess the political risk.

Yeltsin has already handed some powers to Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, who is expected to assume the president's mantle while Yeltsin undergoes surgery. If Yeltsin were to die or be incapacitated, Chernomyrdin would step in for three months until fresh elections could be held.
But one fund manager addressing the conference said he believed it was likely Yeltsin would cling to office for as long as he could.
"Yeltsin will be under intense pressure to hold onto power," said Gordon Muir-Carby, fund manager for Creditanstalt Investment Ltd.

"It is likely he will stay "de jure" president for as long as possible, waiting for the time when (Kremlin security chief Alexander) Lebed's popularity wears off," he said, adding this would give Chernomyrdin time to strengthen his hand.
But Yeltsin's term in office is limited, raising more questions for potential investors.

"The surgeon's statement at the weekend (implying that Yeltsin's health was poorer than hitherto believed) has in effect doomed his second term, and younger men are waiting to take over," Muir-Carby said. "The question is -- will this generation's commitment to economic orthodoxy be as robust?" --London Newsroom +44 171 542 2734
